title: Financing Structure and Startup Survival Under an Exogenous Shock: Does Debt Buffer While Founder Equity Amplifies Exit Risk? Evidence from an Emerging Economy
content: This paper examines whether the survival value of different financing sources is contingent on exposure to an exogenous shock. We assemble hand-collected survey data on 301 startups founded during 2021–2022 across five provinces of Vietnam's Mekong Delta—a peripheral entrepreneurial ecosystem within a bank-based emerging economy—and track them for up to 56 months, observing 114 market exits. Cox proportional hazards models show that external finance is protective: debt, angel investment, and family-and-friends funding significantly reduce the exit hazard, whereas re-liance on founder equity increases it; government financial support has no detectable effect. Criti-cally, these effects are concentrated almost entirely among Covid-exposed ventures. Within the exposed cohort, a one-log-unit increase in founder-equity funding is associated with a more than four-fold exit hazard (HR = 4.51; p = 0.001), while debt reduces the hazard by roughly a quarter per log-unit (HR = 0.77; p < 0.001); among non-exposed ventures, financing composition is essentially unrelated to survival. Discrete-time, matching, and logistic estimates corroborate these patterns. The findings challenge the view of debt as a source of fragility for young firms and indicate that financing structure operates as a crisis-contingent resource, with implications for founders, lenders, and the design of startup support policy in emerging economies.
